name: Iris Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I study marketing and management, and honestly I'm all in. A normal week is lectures in the morning, then I'm at the campus co-working space building social posts for my parents' bakery and two other small cafes. My parents run a bakery called Casa Garcia, and I've started doing their Instagram and the online orders. I use AI constantly, for captions, image ideas, summaries, even planning my week. I live in a flat share with two friends, and my parents cover about half the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, we get on with our lives. AI is a handy assistant, not a revolution. I'd tell my friends it's still useful, so keep using it. Online I wouldn't post much, since I'd rather show the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be a bit let down, because it's more fun when it's huge. But my plan doesn't need a revolution. A marketing degree and real clients is a decent path whatever AI does. I'd be calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on building clients. I'd go from three to six small businesses by the end of the year and charge a bit more. I'd also apply for a summer job at an agency. I'd keep the AI tools but also learn analytics properly, so I'm not just a captions person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit impatient, I think. I like momentum, and a plateau feels slow. But there's nothing to fear in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI constantly. If it turns out to be a plateau, what changes for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd just carry on being the person who knows both marketing and the tools, which makes me useful. If AI is slow, that edge lasts longer, so it's not bad for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the bakery's situation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bakery's doing okay. We've got regulars and weekend queues, but margins are thin because of flour and electricity. My income from the small clients helps a little, and I'm putting some aside for second-year rent. If the plateau means stable prices, that's good for them.

say: I'd say we get on with our lives, because AI is a **handy assistant** and not a revolution.
I'd show the work instead of posting opinions.
think: I'd be a bit **let down**, but a marketing degree with real clients works whatever AI does.
do: Grow from three to **six** small business clients by the end of the year.
Apply for a summer job at a **marketing agency**.
Learn **analytics** properly so I'm not just the captions person.
feel: **Calm** and a little impatient, because a plateau feels slow.
S0.quote: A marketing degree and real clients is a decent path whatever AI does.
fieldNote: Calm because she already has **paying clients** and her family's bakery to learn from.
Impatience is a character trait rather than a worry.
Her income is small but it is her own, which matters to her.

steps.text: Grow from three to six small business clients this year
Apply for a summer job at a marketing agency
Take an online analytics course beyond just captions

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's exciting and that people who learn the tools will do well. I'd say that to the student business society and at the bakery. I'd also say the tools shouldn't just serve big companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I know the entry-level agency jobs would go, because a lot of that is captions, reports and scheduling. But I already do those things with AI, and I know how to sell. So I'd feel ahead of most of my classmates, but not safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd double the client work and move into higher-value stuff like strategy and branding, where clients pay for judgement. I'd build a portfolio with real numbers, such as the bakery's online sales going up by a third. I'd join a startup society and take a data module. I'd also save a bit from every invoice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and slightly uneasy. I like being fast, but I know it can turn quickly if everyone's fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Marketing is mostly writing and planning, which this card hits. How do you see that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The people who gain are those who can use the tools and understand customers. People who lose are those who only did the routine bits, like junior copywriters. I'd worry for some of my coursemates who don't use AI. They think it's cheating.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who gains and who loses?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to help them, in a casual way. I'd show them how I do my planning. But some won't listen. Honestly, I'd like to turn that into something, like a small workshop for other students.

say: I'd say it's **exciting** and the tools shouldn't only serve big companies.
I'd say that at the business society and at the bakery.
think: Entry-level agency jobs would go, but I already work with AI and know how to **sell**.
I'd feel ahead of classmates but **not safe**.
do: Double client work and move into **strategy** and branding.
Build a **portfolio** with numbers, like the bakery's online sales up by a third.
Take a **data module** and save part of every invoice.
feel: **Excited** and slightly uneasy, because speed is only an edge until everyone's fast.
S1.quote: I like being fast, but I know it can turn quickly if everyone's fast.
fieldNote: Sees herself ahead, but names the **catch**: speed stops being an edge.
Idea of running a workshop for classmates shows entrepreneurial instinct.
Her portfolio plan is concrete, built around the bakery numbers.

steps.text: Double my client work and sell branding and strategy
Add the bakery's online sales numbers to my portfolio
Take a data module in second semester
Run a small AI workshop for coursemates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it changes everything, and that we need rules and support fast. I'd say I'm going to keep using AI, but we also need basic protections. I'd say it directly to people, not rant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be scared. If AI does all the thinking work, a marketing degree isn't worth much, and neither is my freelance work. By 2028 I'd be in second year, and I'd be graduating into a world with nothing for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the time to build something I own. I'd turn my client work into a proper small business, with AI doing the routine and me selling trust. I'd also help my parents add a website shop and local delivery. I'd save every pound I can. And I'd think hard about whether to finish the degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's fast, and I can't plan for it properly. But I wouldn't freeze. I'd rather be doing something than waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is very fast. What happens to a marketing student?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my parents the bakery's safe longer, because baking is hands-on until about 2031. People still want bread made by someone. I'd push them to use AI for ordering and for the shop's promotions, and maybe sell more online. I'd be the person bringing the new tools in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents about the bakery?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably still finish the degree, because I'd regret quitting. But I'd care less about grades and more about customers and income. In a world like that, having a business and a network is probably worth more than a certificate.

say: I'd say it changes everything and we need **rules and support** fast.
I'd keep using AI, but I'd say it directly, not rant.
think: If AI does all the thinking work, my degree and my freelance work are worth **much less**.
I'd graduate into a world with **nothing** for me.
do: Turn my client work into a proper small **business**, with AI doing the routine.
Help my parents add a **website shop** and local delivery.
Think hard about whether to finish the **degree**.
feel: **Anxious**, but I wouldn't freeze, because I'd rather be doing something.
S2.quote: In a world like that, having a business and a network is probably worth more than a certificate.
fieldNote: Responds to fear with **action**, building something she owns.
Takes the bakery's hands-on advantage seriously and wants to bring tools in.
Willing to question the degree, rare for someone with good grades.

steps.text: Register my client work as a proper small business
Build a website shop and local delivery for the bakery
Save every spare pound from client invoices
Think hard about whether to finish the degree

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's enough time to get ready, and that I'm going to use every year. I'd also say we need training programmes for people who lose their work, funded properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think I could probably get a good first job, and two years in a business gives me contacts and proof I can do it. By 2031 I might be running my own agency. It's a risk, but one I can see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, take a job in a fast-growing business for two years, and save hard. I'd launch my own small agency on the side before 2031. I'd also learn enough about automation tools that I can sell them to small firms. And I'd pay for my own training with the income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly uneasy, not scared. There's time and I like having a mission.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years gives you the degree and a first job. How do you use it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd add online ordering to the bakery, and gradually bring in automated stock and ordering. That would let my parents cut costs. I'd also persuade them to keep a human face for the shop, because that's what people come for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about your parents' bakery in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years, I have time to be a player, not a bystander. In two years I'm racing to keep up. That makes this one feel quite positive, to be honest. It's the one I'd choose.

say: I'd say there's **enough time** to get ready and I'd use every year.
I'd say training programmes must be funded properly.
think: Two years in a business gives me **contacts** and proof I can do the work.
By 2031 I might be running my own **agency**, which is a visible risk.
do: Finish the degree, work **two years** in a fast-growing business and save hard.
Launch a small **agency** on the side before 2031.
Learn **automation tools** to sell to small firms.
feel: Mostly **uneasy**, not scared, because I like having a mission.
S3.quote: With five years, I have time to be a player, not a bystander.
fieldNote: Time reads as **opportunity**, which fits her adaptive streak.
Plans for the bakery balance automation with keeping a human face.
Candid that this is the scenario she would choose.

steps.text: Work two years in a fast-growing business after graduating
Launch a small agency on the side before 2031
Learn automation tools to sell to small firms
Add automated ordering to the bakery

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have time to do it right, and I'd tell my friends to build skills, not panic. I'd also say the usual institutions should use the decade to retrain people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be calm, to be honest. In ten years I could have two careers. I could work in marketing, build a business, then move into something new. By 2036 I'd be 28, not old. That's a good place to start from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build the agency slowly, graduate, work, and probably start my own thing by 25. I'd invest in a small index fund each month, and maybe buy into the bakery. I'd take extra courses in whatever the market asks for. And I'd keep using AI, because it's now like using a phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like knowing what's coming and having a good map. It doesn't scare me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a different shape. What would you do with it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the government to fund training, sort out how people get support if they lose work, and make sure that smaller companies can use AI, not just big ones. That's the fair way to do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from the government in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the one I'd feel best in, to be honest, because I could be early to everything. But I'd want to still help the people who aren't as quick, like my parents. I'd teach them the tools in the bakery.

say: I'd say we have **time** to do it right and I'd tell friends to build skills, not panic.
I'd say institutions should use the decade to retrain people.
think: In ten years I could have **two careers**, and at 28 I'd not be old.
do: Build the agency slowly and start my own thing by **25**.
Put money in an **index fund** each month and maybe buy into the bakery.
Take **extra courses** in whatever the market asks for.
feel: **Calm**, like knowing what's coming and having a good map.
S4.quote: I'd want the government to fund training, sort out how people get support if they lose work, and make sure that smaller companies can use AI, not just big ones.
fieldNote: Calm comes from **time and confidence** in her own ability to adapt.
Still holds a fairness view about small firms getting access.
Wants to help her parents adopt tools, tying her optimism to family.

steps.text: Start my own marketing business by age twenty-five
Invest monthly in an index fund from client income
Teach my parents the AI tools at the bakery

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most, because I'd have the least time and the least built. What would help is something like funded training and easy ways to start a small business, and for banks and the government to back young people who try. I don't need a handout, I need a runway.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I'd like to say young people aren't one group. Some of us are really excited and some are terrified, and most are both on different days. I'm mostly excited, but I know that's partly luck.

headlineQuote: I don't need a handout, I need a runway.
portrait: **Iris Garcia** is 18, a marketing and management student who runs social media for her parents' bakery and other small clients.
She uses **AI every day** and treats it like a phone, a tool she already trusts.
Her mood stays calm in a plateau and a ten-year warning, and rises to anxious in a two-year AGI.
She answers fear with action, building her own **small business** and portfolio.
She wants funded training and a runway for young people, and wants to teach her parents the tools.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI scenario worries her most, with the least time and the least built.
whatWouldHelp: She wants funded training and easy ways to start a small business, with backing for young people, not a **handout**.
